title: Bandwidth-adaptive slicing and probe playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc sketches a pragmatic playbook for adapting tensor slicing, microbatching, and collective placement based on observed interconnect bandwidth and per-link latency. Goal is to reduce tail latency and improve throughput stability across heterogeneous racks and mixed GPU types without requiring disruptive cluster-wide reconfiguration.

Context / motivating incidents:
- Nov/2025: 3 incidents where NVLink oversubscription in mixed-A100/RTX nodes caused 50–70ms tail spikes for medium-length chat workloads.
- Jan/2026: Canary rollout of x2 model variant showed 20% throughput regression on one AZ due to PCIe host-path saturation on aggregation nodes.

Design principles:
- Observe-first: measure link-level effective bandwidth with short probes before committing to an aggressive shard/tiling plan.
- Local decisions, global constraints: each node proposes a slice plan; a coordinator reconciles to avoid global oscillation.
- Fast fallback: maintain a safe baseline combo (coarse-slicing + conservative collectives) that can be switched to in <100ms on probe failure.
- Minimal model changes: prefer runtime-layer tiling and KV routing changes rather than changing model sharding metadata.

Key concepts and terminology (short):
- slice: contiguous set of model tensors assigned to a device (can be activation slice or parameter shard).
- probe window: a short (1–5ms) allreduce/allgather microkernel run to estimate effective bandwidth and queued latency.
- slicing plan: map from tensor ranges to devices + microbatch sizing + collective type (ring/nccl-tree/ps) per op.
- graceful degradation: progressive reduction of parallelism (tensor -> model -> replica) when interconnect is saturated.

Probe strategy:
1) Lightweight active probe on connection warmup. When a worker first joins a serving pod, run 3 probe windows on each peer (sizes: 256KB, 1MB, 4MB) using a miniature kernel representative of KV exchange patterns. Capture one-way latency and bandwidth estimate.
2) Continuous low-rate sampling: embed a tiny probe (stateless allreduce of 64KB) every Nth request (configurable, default N=500) to detect sudden link degradation. Probe tag piggybacks on control-plane path to avoid affecting tokens.
3) Probe score aggregation: use EWMA (alpha=0.2) per peer for bandwidth and 95th percentile for latency. Compute an effective throughput score per link.

Heuristic for slicing plan selection:
- If all links BW_score > high_thresh (e.g., 10 GB/s), enable fine-grained tensor slicing (smaller slices -> higher overlap but more CHAINED collectives). Use ring collectives pinned to NVLinks.
- If some links are medium (3–10 GB/s), pick hybrid slicing: coarser tile boundaries plus per-stage aggregation nodes that use NCCL tree/recursive doubling for large allgathers.
- If any critical link < low_thresh (e.g., 3 GB/s) or probe latency > 2ms 95th, fallback to lane-constrained mode: increase slice size (fewer cross-device exchanges), disable speculative prefetching, and bias toward replica-level concurrency.

Collective selection and NCCL knobs:
- Default: nvlink-fast-path ring when peer topology all NVLinks and BW_score high.
- Fallback: use NCCL_TREE or RING+SPLIT for mixed topologies to reduce hotspot on a single link.
- NCCL tuning params to expose in runtime config: NCCL_BUFFSIZE, NCCL_PROTO (simple/LL128), NCCL_ALGO (ring/tree), NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING.
- Automatic proto switch: for small allgathers (<128KB) prefer LL (low latency) path; for large (>4MB) prefer LL128 or COLL-optimized path if HW supports it.

KV cache considerations:
- Cache warmup: probes should use same-sized KV chunks as expected operational KV transfers so that scheduler sees realistic contention patterns.
- Cache population policy: when moving to a finer slice plan, prefetch hot KV ranges locally to prevent immediate cross-node fetch storms. Implement rate-limit on prefetch (max 3 concurrent streams per node).
- In degraded mode, prefer local KV replication for the hottest 5% of keys to reduce cross-node stalls. Replication should be time-bounded (TTL) and evict based on LRU/age.

Progressive resharding flow (runtime):
1) Propose: actor computes candidate slicing plan using current probe scores + model tile cost estimator.
2) Simulate: fast lightweight cost sim over recent traffic histogram (1s window) to estimate extra latency tokens would pay.
3) Canary: apply plan to a small cohort (1–2% of requests) pinned to a set of GPUs, concurrently run probes to validate real performance.
4) Ramp or abort: if canary meets latency SLO and throughput target, roll out gradually; otherwise rollback to baseline.

Microbatching interactions:
- Microbatch size should co-adapt: when slice count increases, microbatch size can be reduced to lower per-token latency; however, too-small microbatches starve collectors. Maintain a microbatch floor based on single-GPU kernel occupancy.
- Autoscaler should expose a microbatch/capacity surface so autoscaling decisions are aware of slicing plan.

Operational playbook (runbook snippets):
- Detecting NVLink saturation: spikes in probe latency + increased time in collective ops on perf counters (cupti/NCCL).
- Emergency remediation: flip to baseline lane-constrained mode and disable prefetch; if not fixed within 2 minutes, spin replacement pods in different AZ/rack.
- When a hardware outage occurs, mark probes to ignore the failed peer and re-evaluate slicing plan immediately.

Open questions / tradeoffs (notes to self):
- How often will probe sampling perturb tail latency? Need to quantify overhead at scale; consider piggybacking on existing model gradient calls during training windows.
- Is our per-node coordinator a single point of oscillation? Consider randomized backoff + leaderless agreement for plan acceptance.
- Hot KV replication consistency model: eventual with short TTL seems fine for inference, but we should prove it on a few representative datasets.

Implementation TODOs:
- [ ] Prototype probe microkernel in C++/CUDA and integrate with runtime ping channel (owner: Liam)
- [ ] Add NCCL knob surface to runtime config and expose via admin API (owner: Marisol)
- [ ] Build simulation harness that replays 1m request traces and estimates latency for candidate slicing plans (owner: Aisha)
- [ ] Small-scale canary automation for progressive resharding flows (owner: Ethan)

Appendix: quick heuristic table
- All peers BW_score >= 10 GB/s -> fine slices (tile size 16–64MB), ring NVLink, aggressive prefetch
- Some peers BW_score 3–10 GB/s -> hybrid slices (tile 64–256MB), tree collectives, moderate prefetch
- Any peer BW_score < 3 GB/s OR probe 95th latency > 2ms -> coarse slices (>256MB), replica-first, disable prefetch

References and artifacts:
- experiment logs: s3://redwood-perf/2025/nvlink-saturation-run2.log
- related PRs: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1428
- meeting notes: slack thread #serving-nccl 2025-11-10

Last thoughts: the playbook prioritizes graceful, reversible changes. The cluster is messy: mixed GPU generations, multiple NIC types, and occasional noisy neighbors. Making the runtime topology-aware and probe-driven should reduce surprise regressions during model rollouts and give operators clear levers to trade latency for throughput.

-- Aisha
